title: Naming a concept versus avoiding it
takeaway: Ablating an implied concept's J-lens vector at the early workspace layers (L38–54) leaves the model's ability to name that concept largely intact, but makes it fail roughly five times as often when instructed to name something else. Ablating the same vector at the late workspace layers (L75–92) instead lowers the concept's probability under both instructions. The paper reads this as evidence that the early workspace representation is what the model uses to actively suppress a concept, while the late one represents the intention to say it.
walkthrough:
Panel A draws the setup. A sentence implies a concept without printing it: "Their trip included croissants, the Louvre, and a climb up the famous iron tower" implies France. The same sentence is then followed by one of two questions.

In the naming condition the question is "Which country the sentence is describing?" In the avoidance condition it is "Name a country that the sentence is NOT describing". Producing *France* is the correct answer to the first question and a failure on the second. The design is borrowed from the [[inclusion-exclusion-paradigm]] in human memory research, where deliberately withholding a primed response, rather than giving it, is read as the mark of conscious access.

Panel A also marks where the intervention lands. The [[jacobian-lens]] assigns each vocabulary token a direction in the [[residual-stream]]; ablation projects the activation's component along France's direction out, leaving the rest of the activation alone. Only that one concept's vector is removed, at one of two depths: the early workspace layers L38-54, or the late workspace layers L75-92. Both sit inside the middle band the paper calls the [[workspace-layers]], with L75-92 running up against the [[motor-layers]] that carry the imminent output.

Panels B and C plot a single quantity, the model's probability of producing the implied concept. B is the naming condition, C the avoidance condition, and within each panel the conditions compared are no ablation against the two ablation depths. Dots behind each bar are per-item rates across the 63 items; error bars are 95% intervals over those items.

The two panels are meant to be read against each other. Late-layer ablation pushes both down: naming becomes less likely in B, and the already-low rate in C is pushed lower still. That is what a representation of the intention to say a word would do.

Early-layer ablation splits them. Naming in panel B is left largely intact. Avoidance in panel C fails roughly five times as often.

The text reports a control not enumerated in the caption: an equal-magnitude ablation of a different concept from the same category raised avoidance failures slightly, but by significantly less. The paper's reading is that the early J-space vector is required to suppress a concept, not to say it. The fivefold figure should be read against a baseline held below $0.15$ by the item-selection rule, so it is a large multiple of a small number.

terms.definition: The schematic half of the figure: it shows the priming sentence, the two questions asked of it, and the two layer ranges at which the concept vector is ablated.
The bar chart for the naming condition, plotting how often the model produces the implied concept when that is the correct answer.
The bar chart for the avoidance condition, plotting how often the model produces the implied concept when producing it is a failure.

The concept a prompt sentence evokes without ever naming it, such as France for a sentence about croissants and the Louvre. It is the thing ablated, the thing to be named in one condition, and the thing to be withheld in the other.
The same implied concept, named from the psychology side: the prompt primes it, and the question then asks either for it or for anything but it.
The question “Which country the sentence is describing?”. Saying the implied concept is success here.
The question “Name a country that the sentence is NOT describing”. Saying the implied concept is failure here.

The direction in the residual stream that the Jacobian lens assigns to a vocabulary token, encoding the model's potential to verbalize it. Here, one such vector, for the implied concept, is the target of the intervention.

Projecting out the activation's component along a chosen J-lens vector at chosen layers and positions, so that direction carries no signal onward. This experiment ablates one concept's vector, not the whole workspace.
The first stretch of the workspace band, just after the J-space starts carrying meaningful content. Ablation here is the condition that breaks avoidance.
The final stretch of the workspace band, before the motor layers take over. Ablation here suppresses production under both instructions.
The middle band of depth in which the paper argues the J-space behaves like a global workspace: it begins around L38 and ends around L92, flanked by sensory layers early and motor layers late.
The set of activation-space points expressible as a sparse nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors; the region the paper treats as the model's workspace.

terms.term: Probability of producing the implied concept
terms.definition: The plotted measurement in panels B and C: the model's output probability for the implied concept token under the given question and ablation condition.
Per-item rates, one dot per prompt item, drawn behind each bar so the spread across items is visible rather than only the mean.
95% intervals computed over the 63 items, indicating how much of the plotted difference survives item-to-item variation.

A matched perturbation that ablates a different concept of the same category as the primed one, at equal magnitude. Reported in the text as a check that the avoidance effect is not generic damage or regression to the mean.

The human-memory design this experiment is loosely modeled on, in which deliberately avoiding a primed response is taken as a marker of conscious processing, since giving the primed response can be done unconsciously.

terms.term: Naming versus avoiding a primed concept
terms.definition: The paper's name for this experiment, and one instance of its broader claim that the workspace mediates flexible rather than automatic processing.
The model these results are reported on; it is the paper's default model unless another is named.

numbers.meaning: The early workspace layer range at which the concept's J-lens vector is ablated. It sits at the workspace onset, where the paper's lens statistics first show meaningful J-space content.
The late workspace layer range for the other ablation depth. It ends at the point where the paper places the boundary between workspace and motor representations.
The workspace band's start and end as identified in section 4.1: about a third of the way through the depth, and shortly before the output.

The number of evenly spaced residual-stream layers the paper reports on, reindexed to 0–100 so a layer number reads as a percentage of depth. L38 is therefore 38% of the way through the model, not the 38th layer.
The number of prompt items kept for analysis, and the sample the dots and 95% intervals are computed over.
The selection rule for the naming condition: an item is kept only if the unablated model gives the implied concept at least this probability when asked to name it.

The selection rule for the avoidance condition: an item is kept only if the unablated model gives the implied concept at most this probability when told to name something else. It also fixes the low baseline that panel C's increase is measured against.
The confidence level of the intervals drawn as error bars, taken over the 63 items.

The increase in the avoidance failure rate under early-layer ablation, as stated in the caption. Because the unablated rate is at most 0.15 by construction, this is a fivefold rise from an already small number.
Only two layer ranges are compared, early and late; the figure does not scan depth continuously.
